seoTitle: Common Appliance Problems and When to Call a Pro
seoDescription: The symptoms homeowners see most often, the checks that are safe to do yourself, and the point where an appliance repair professional should take over.
excerpt: Most appliance failures announce themselves before they stop working. Here are the symptoms worth acting on, the checks that are safe to do yourself, and the point where a technician should take over.
seoSummary: Diagnostic guide to the ten most common appliance failures, with a safe-to-check / call-a-pro split.
author: Safe Home Network Editorial
visual: Flat vector scene: technician with a multimeter at an open oven, homeowner holding a manual, warm kitchen background.

paras: An appliance rarely fails without warning. A fridge runs a little longer, a washer thumps on the spin cycle, an oven takes twenty minutes to reach temperature. Those small changes are the cheapest moment to act, because the repair is usually a part rather than the whole machine.

This guide covers the failures homeowners report most often, what each symptom usually points to, and which checks are genuinely safe to do yourself. It also explains when stopping and calling a qualified appliance technician is the cheaper and safer decision.

One rule applies to every appliance in this article: anything that involves gas, a sealed refrigerant circuit, or opening a panel that exposes mains wiring is a job for a professional. The rest is about gathering evidence so the conversation with a technician starts from facts.

sections.h2: Start with the three questions that solve most cases
paras: Before diagnosing anything, answer three questions. They remove a surprising share of service calls that turn out to be user error or a household supply problem.
ordered: **Is it receiving power?** Check the plug is fully seated, the socket works with another device, and the breaker has not tripped. For a gas appliance, confirm the gas supply was not shut off during other work.
**Is it receiving water or drainage?** Dishwashers and washing machines fail on a kinked inlet hose or a blocked standpipe at least as often as on a pump.
**Did anything change?** A new outlet strip, a kitchen remodel, a power cut, a moved appliance, a filter change — most "it just stopped" stories have a trigger.
sections.note: Never pull an appliance out by its cord, and never test a socket with a screwdriver. A plug-in socket tester costs a few dollars and removes the guesswork.

paras: If a refrigerator or air conditioner has lost refrigerant, the system has a leak, and the leak must be found and repaired before recharging. Topping up a leaking system is a temporary fix that damages the compressor. This work needs certification and gauges — it is never a homeowner task.

sections.h2: Repair or replace? A decision homeowners can make
paras: The industry rule of thumb is simple enough to use: multiply the appliance's age by the repair cost, and compare the result with the price of a comparable new unit. Above roughly half the replacement price, replacement usually wins — especially for appliances already past their expected service life.

That rule is a starting point, not a verdict. Efficiency matters too: a fifteen-year-old refrigerator can use meaningfully more electricity than a current model, which changes the maths over a few years. Rebates and tax incentives for efficient appliances vary by state and utility, so check locally before assuming a new unit costs the full sticker price.

head: Appliance
Typical service life
Repair usually sensible when…
rows: Under 10 years old and the sealed system is intact
A pump, valve or control board, not a leaking tub
The duct is clear and the drum turns freely
A heating element, igniter or thermostat
Rarely worth repairing beyond a fuse or door switch

sections.h2: The checks worth doing before you book a visit
bullets: Write down the exact model and serial number — it is on a plate inside the door or behind the kick panel, and it determines part availability.
Record the symptom with a short video, including any sound the machine makes.
Note what you already tried so the technician is not billed for repeating it.
Confirm the appliance is level and the door seals sit flush; a misaligned door is a common and cheap fix.
Ask whether the company's diagnostic fee is credited against the repair — a fair policy either way, but it should be stated up front.

sections.h2: When to stop and call a professional
paras: Stop immediately if you smell gas, see scorched wiring, notice water pooling near an electrical component, or the breaker trips every time the appliance runs. Unplug the appliance if you can reach the plug safely and call a qualified technician or your gas utility.

Also call for anything behind a sealed panel, anything involving refrigerant, and any repair that requires moving a unit heavier than you can handle safely. Appliance injuries are usually back injuries or cuts from sharp sheet-metal edges, both avoidable.
sections.note: If the appliance is still under a manufacturer warranty, call the manufacturer's authorised service first. Opening the cabinet yourself can void the warranty.

faqs.q: How much does an appliance repair usually cost?
faqs.a: Pricing depends entirely on the appliance, the part and your market, so any national figure is a guess. Ask for the diagnostic fee, whether it is credited against the repair, and the parts-and-labour price in writing before work begins. Compare the quote with the replacement cost of a comparable unit — that comparison matters more than the absolute number.

faqs.q: Is it worth repairing a 12-year-old appliance?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the machine is otherwise sound and the fault is a single inexpensive part, repair can buy several more years. If the repair approaches half the price of a new unit, or the appliance is already past its expected service life, replacement is usually the better use of the money.

faqs.q: Can I repair my own appliances?
faqs.a: You can safely do the external checks: power, water, filters, seals, level, and clearing lint or debris. Anything that requires opening a panel, touching a capacitor, working on a gas line or handling refrigerant should be left to a qualified technician — microwave capacitors in particular can hold a lethal charge long after the unit is unplugged.

faqs.q: Why did the technician ask for the model number first?
faqs.a: Because the same symptom can need a different part on different revisions of the same model. The model and serial number identify the exact build, which is what makes a first-visit repair possible instead of a second appointment.

seoTitle: Refrigerator Not Cooling? 8 Causes and What to Check
seoDescription: Fridge warm but freezer cold? Work through the safe causes first — airflow, seals, coils and controls — then learn which faults need a certified technician.
excerpt: A refrigerator that runs but will not cool is usually one of eight things. Start with the checks that cost nothing, then decide whether the sealed system needs a professional.
seoSummary: Ordered troubleshooting guide for a refrigerator that is not cooling, with a clear stop line before refrigerant work.
author: Safe Home Network Editorial
visual: Flat vector: open fridge with a warm-air wavy line, thermometer reading, coils behind the unit.

paras: The refrigerator is the one appliance where the failure costs money by the hour. Before anything else: if the interior is above 40°F (4°C), food safety becomes the priority. Perishables that have been above that temperature for more than about two hours are better discarded than risked — and that decision should be made before you start troubleshooting.

Once the food is dealt with, the cause is usually one of eight things. Four are safe and sensible for a homeowner to check. Four involve sealed-system or electrical work that belongs with a qualified appliance technician.

Cold air is produced in the freezer and travels into the fresh-food compartment through a vent, often driven by a fan. Overload the shelves, push a cereal box against the vent, or let the freezer fill to the door and the fridge section stops receiving cold air. The symptom is unmistakable: the freezer is fine, the fridge is warm.
Pull everything away from the vents, leave a couple of inches of clearance at the back, and give the unit a few hours. If the fridge recovers, nothing is broken — the layout was.

A seal that does not sit flush lets warm, humid room air in continuously. The compressor runs without ever catching up, and you may notice condensation or frost near the door frame. Test with the dollar-bill trick: close the door on a note and pull gently at several points. It should resist all the way around; a spot that slides out freely is a gap.
Clean the gasket with warm soapy water, check the door is level and that the hinges have not sagged. Replacement gaskets are inexpensive and are a reasonable homeowner job on most models.

Coils at the back or underneath the unit shed heat into the room. When they are caked in dust and pet hair, heat cannot escape and cooling performance drops — often worst in summer, which is when people notice. Vacuum the coils with a brush attachment and clear the gap around the cabinet.
This is one of the few genuinely valuable maintenance tasks on a refrigerator, and it also reduces energy use. Do it twice a year with pets in the house.

It sounds trivial until it happens: a child has turned the temperature dial, a demo mode is on, or the control panel was bumped during cleaning. Check the set point against the manual, confirm the unit is not in a display or vacation mode, and look for an error code on the panel.

Also confirm the appliance is plugged into a working socket — a fridge on a switched outlet that someone switched off will run on nothing at all. A refrigerator that is completely silent with the light on points at the control board rather than cooling.

The evaporator fan moves air across the cold coil. When it fails, the freezer may still be cold but the fridge section warms, and you may hear nothing where you previously heard a hum. Some models show a fan error code.

You can listen for the fan by opening the freezer door and pressing the door switch; if the fan does not spin up and there is no obstruction, the motor or its control is at fault. Replacement requires dismantling the freezer interior, which is a technician job on most models.

A defrost system failure lets ice coat the evaporator until airflow stops entirely. Symptoms include a fridge that gradually warms over days, frost visible at the back of the freezer, and a compressor that runs constantly.

A one-time manual defrost — empty the unit, unplug it, leave the doors open for 24 hours with towels down — will restore cooling temporarily. If the problem returns within weeks, the defrost heater, thermostat or timer needs replacement. That is a technician repair, not a permanent fix.

If the compressor tries to start, clicks, and stops, the start relay may have failed. Sometimes the compressor itself has. You may hear a click every few minutes and feel the side of the cabinet staying cold to the touch.

A failed relay is a modest repair; a failed compressor usually is not, especially on an older unit. A technician diagnoses this with a meter rather than by substitution, which is why it is worth paying for the diagnostic instead of buying parts on suspicion.

A sealed system that has lost refrigerant cannot cool, no matter how clean the coils are. Signs include a compressor that runs continuously without getting warm, no frost pattern on the evaporator, and sometimes an oily residue at a joint.

Refrigerant work requires certification, gauges and a leak search. Recharging a leaking system is not a repair — it is a delay that damages the compressor. If a technician confirms a leak in an accessible component, repair can be worthwhile; if the leak is in the sealed evaporator of an older unit, replacement is usually the honest recommendation.
sections.note: Never add refrigerant or "top up" a domestic refrigerator yourself. It is illegal without certification in the US, and it does not fix the underlying leak.

ordered: Move perishables to a cooler with ice; discard anything that has been warm for hours.
Confirm power, then check the set point and any error code.
Clear vents and rebalance the shelves; test the door seals.
Vacuum the condenser coils and confirm the unit has rear clearance.
If it still will not cool, book a technician and describe the freezer-versus-fridge pattern — that single detail tells them which subsystem to bring parts for.

sections.h2: What the freezer-versus-fridge pattern tells a technician

head: Pattern
Most likely area
Typical next step
rows: Everything warm, compressor hot and running
Frost at the back of the freezer
Cooling returns after a 24-hour defrost, then fails again
Same as above — the defrost is not completing

faqs.q: How long can food stay safe in a fridge that is not cooling?
faqs.a: The USDA guidance is that perishable food should be discarded if it has been above 40°F for more than two hours. A closed refrigerator holds cold for roughly four hours; a full freezer rather longer. When in doubt, throw it out — the cost of replacing food is far lower than the cost of a foodborne illness.

faqs.q: Why is my freezer cold but the refrigerator warm?
faqs.a: That pattern almost always means cold air is not reaching the fresh-food compartment: a blocked vent, a failed evaporator fan, a stuck air damper, or heavy frost from a defrost failure. It is rarely a refrigerant problem, which is good news for the repair bill.

faqs.q: Can I just turn the temperature down to fix it?
faqs.a: Lowering the set point masks a mild airflow or seal problem and makes the compressor run continuously, which wastes energy and shortens its life. Find the cause instead; if the unit cannot hold 37°F at the normal setting, something needs attention.

faqs.q: Is a refrigerator repair worth it on a 10-year-old unit?
faqs.a: Often yes for a fan, relay, thermostat or defrost component. A sealed-system repair on a unit near the end of its 12–15 year life is usually not, because the labour is significant and the rest of the appliance is also ageing. Ask for both numbers before deciding.

seoTitle: How to Choose a Reliable Appliance Repair Service
seoDescription: What separates a good appliance repair company from a bad one: licensing, diagnostic fees, parts policy, warranty terms and the questions worth asking.
excerpt: Diagnostic fees, parts policies, warranty wording and the questions that reveal how a repair company actually works — a practical checklist for choosing well the first time.
seoSummary: Hiring checklist for appliance repair: credentials, fee structures, warranty terms, red flags.
author: Safe Home Network Editorial
visual: Flat vector: homeowner with clipboard comparing two quotes, washing machine and fridge icons, checkmarks.

paras: Appliance repair is one of the few trades where a homeowner often calls someone without any personal reference, in a hurry, with a machine full of food or washing. That combination makes it worth knowing what a good operator looks like before you need one.
This guide is deliberately practical. It covers what to verify, what to ask, how the money usually works, and the specific behaviours that should make you choose someone else.

sections.h2: Verify three things before you book
paras: If your appliance is still under warranty, work by an unauthorised technician can void it. Ask whether the company is authorised for your brand, and check with the manufacturer if the answer is vague. For out-of-warranty work it matters less, but authorisation is a signal that the technician has access to current parts and service documentation.

head: Charge type
What it should mean
What to confirm
rows: Is it credited against the repair if you proceed?
One price for the job, parts included
Does it cover the part, labour, and a return visit if the fault persists?
Hourly labour plus parts at cost or list
What is the hourly rate, and is there a minimum?
Travel only, on top of labour
Is it charged again if parts must be ordered?

paras: None of these structures is inherently dishonest — but the diagnostic fee policy is the one that most often surprises homeowners. A company that credits the fee against the repair is telling you it expects to do the work; a company that charges a full diagnostic and then quotes a separate inflated repair is a different proposition.
Get the total in writing before work starts. A verbal "around two hundred" is not a quote, and it is not enforceable.

ordered: Are you licensed or registered where my state or city requires it, and what is the number?
Do you carry liability insurance and workers' compensation?
Is the diagnostic fee credited if I approve the repair?
Will you give me a written price before starting work?
What warranty do you provide on the part, and separately on the labour?
Do you use original manufacturer parts, and if not, what are you fitting?
If the part has to be ordered, is the return visit charged?
What happens if the same fault returns within 30 days?
sections.note: A good sign is a company that answers these by email without being pushed. A bad sign is irritation at being asked.

sections.h2: Parts policy matters more than people expect
paras: Original equipment manufacturer (OEM) parts fit and carry the manufacturer's quality control. Aftermarket parts are often perfectly serviceable and cheaper, but quality varies widely by category, and some cheap control boards fail quickly.
Ask which is being fitted and what it changes about the warranty. If a company will not tell you, that is the answer.

A typical trade warranty covers the part for 90 days to a year and the labour for 30 to 90 days. The wording matters in three places: whether the warranty covers the part only or the whole repair, whether it is void if you use another company, and whether a repeat visit carries a new trip charge.
Ask for the warranty in writing. If a company offers "a guarantee" with no terms, that guarantee is a mood rather than a promise.

sections.h2: Red flags worth walking away from
bullets: A price quoted over the phone without the model number — it is a number designed to get the visit booked.
Pressure to decide immediately, or a discount that expires while the technician is standing in your kitchen.
Refusal to put the diagnosis or the price in writing.
A diagnosis that changes after the appliance is opened, with no explanation of what was found.
A call centre that cannot name the technician who will arrive or the company's local address.

sections.h2: How to get the best outcome from the visit
bullets: Have the model and serial number ready; it is usually inside the door or behind the kick panel.
Clear access to the appliance and protect the floor.
Describe the symptom precisely: when it starts, what it sounds like, what changed.
Ask the technician to show you the failed part and explain the diagnosis.
Keep the invoice, the warranty terms and any part numbers for future reference.

sections.h2: A short checklist before you say yes
paras: Business name and address confirmed, insurance checked, diagnostic fee policy understood, written price received, parts policy and warranty terms in hand. If any of those is missing, you are not being difficult — you are doing what the company should expect.

faqs.q: Should I use a manufacturer-authorised repair service?
faqs.a: If the appliance is under warranty, yes — authorised service is usually required to keep the warranty valid, and it is often free. Out of warranty, authorisation still means access to current parts and documentation, but a well-reviewed independent technician can be equally good and sometimes quicker.
Yes. Travel and fault-finding are real work, and a fee is reasonable. What matters is that the policy is stated up front and, ideally, credited against the repair if you approve it.

faqs.q: How long should an appliance repair warranty last?
faqs.a: Common terms are 90 days to one year on parts and 30 to 90 days on labour. Anything shorter than 30 days deserves a question; anything longer than a year on labour is unusual and worth reading carefully.

faqs.q: Can I get a repair quote over the phone?
faqs.a: You can usually get a range, not a quote. Exact pricing needs the model number and often a diagnosis. Be wary of a firm price quoted before anyone knows what is wrong — it tends to be revised upward once the appliance is open.
